document.title: Degradation analysis of a combined cycle heat recovery steam generator under full and part load conditions
document.venue: Sustainable Energy Technologies and Assessments 37 (2020) 100587, Elsevier

paragraphs.text: The authors build a theoretical model that simulates Heat Recovery Steam Generator (HRSG) performance and quantifies the percentage degradation of its components across operating loads and conditions. They also introduce a criterion that fixes the actual operating load of the HRSG from the measured variables of the actual test performance (ATP). Model and load criterion are applied to data logged over two years, giving 10 readings per operating month (January and August) per year at each of the 100%, 75% and 50% loads. Unlike other studies in the field, the degradation analysis rests on real logged plant data. Degradation rate grows with time and with load, while ambient conditions show no notable effect. The largest component degradation, −6.73%, occurs in the low-pressure stage at full load, and the largest overall HRSG degradation is −6.02% at full load. Keywords: Degradation analysis; Modeling analysis; Combined cycle; Heat recovery steam generator.

Energy demand keeps rising [1], increasing the need for efficient and cleaner energy resources [2]. Combined cycle gas turbine (CCGT) plants have shown high energy efficiency thanks to low capital investment, quick load following, flexible operation and lower emissions, though their reliability depends on how available and durable the gas turbine (GT) engine is [3,4], whose heat turns condensate into steam in the heat recovery steam generators (HRSGs). To raise overall plant efficiency a CCGT joins the Brayton and Rankine cycles [5]: one or more GTs are paired with one or more HRSGs, and each HRSG passes GT exhaust heat to condensate from the condenser to raise steam [6] that drives the steam turbine (ST).

Much research targets better CCGT performance and lower fuel use, pollutant emissions and operating cost. Najjar et al. [3,7–10] reviewed combined cycle types, repowering and conversion of steam plants to CCGT, and integrated gasification. Ong'iro et al. [11] built a numerical HRSG model for advanced power cycles, validated it with real HRSG data, predicted pressure drop and temperature profile, and showed that HRSG performance strongly influences overall CCGT performance. Sharma and Singh [12] performed exergy analysis of a dual pressure HRSG while varying dead state temperature, concluding that at higher dead state temperatures the choice of dual pressure condition is critical, that dead state temperature markedly affects exergy losses and efficiencies of the Low-pressure (LP) and High-pressure (HP) steam sections, and that the HRSG carries the largest exergy losses. In other work [13] they found that fin height and density can affect LP evaporator exergy losses and improve LP economizer exergy efficiency.

CCGT components suffer many failure types [14]; HRSGs can deteriorate through corrosion, erosion, metal loss and low cycle fatigue. Failure types, causes, mechanisms and monitoring are treated in many papers [15,16], and close performance monitoring is important for correcting HRSG degradation. Zwebek and Pilidis [17] examined how ST and HRSG component degradation affects CCGT performance, covering reduced overall heat transfer coefficients of the condenser, evaporator, economizer and superheater, ST fouling, ST erosion, lower ST isentropic efficiency and higher GT backpressure; using a FORTRAN simulation with component degradation varied over a percentage range, they found HRSG evaporator degradation to be the most influential fault on the steam cycle, while ST component degradation affects CCGT performance more than the HRSG and condenser.

Cafaro et al. [18] studied degradation of a three pressure level HRSG with a dedicated Matlab code computing actual and expected component effectiveness to form non-dimensional indexes, using three years of logged data; the evaporator proved more prone to degradation than the economizer and superheater. Prior work has thus estimated HRSG degradation rates, but mostly via simulation or theory rather than modeling actual data from an operating plant. The novelty here is to study HRSG and component degradation for a real plant using two years of field data, and to assess the degradation effect on each component and on overall HRSG performance.

The paper therefore examines degradation of the components of a Jordanian combined cycle HRSG, namely the boiler feed pump (BFP), the low-pressure heat recovery steam generator (LP-HRSG) and the high-pressure heat recovery steam generator (HP-HRSG), plus the overall HRSG, at full and part load while the plant ran on back-up diesel fuel. The methodology is applied to historical logged data gathered in January and August over two operating years (2012–2013), during which no washing or maintenance was done on any component. The aim is to support a suitable maintenance schedule, sustained high-efficiency running, minimal downtime, identification of the components most affected by degradation, and lower labor and parts replacement cost, improving overall plant economics.

The plant lies in the southern desert, with hot summers and fairly cold winters; plant data were recorded at night through the year. The area has little industry, so peak demand comes from evening lighting, summer air conditioning and winter heating. HRSG process description: the plant is a conventional CCGT made up mainly of two GT engines rated 168 MW, two-pressure (HP and low-pressure LP) horizontal flow HRSGs, a single-casing two-stage ST rated 130 MW, an air-cooled condenser (ACC) and associated equipment (Fig. 1). It normally runs in combined cycle mode at full and part loads, and bypass stacks and dumpers on the GTs allow simple cycle operation with one or both GTs.

Fig. 1. Plant layout with the HRSG components (legend: BFPⓐ/BFPⓑ boiler feed pumps of steam heat generators 1 and 2; HRSGⓐ/HRSGⓑ HRSGs serving steam turbine engines 1 and 2; HPSH/LPSH high- and low-pressure superheaters; HPST/LPST high- and low-pressure steam turbines; CEP pump for condensate extraction; points 1–4: compressor inlet, combustor outlet, gas turbine inlet and outlet; 5/6: high-pressure HRSG inlet/outlet; 7/8: low-pressure HRSG inlet/outlet; 9/10: preheater inlet/outlet).

The HRSG under study lies inside the dashed box of Fig. 1; GT exhaust passes through the HRSGs, where it heats, boils and superheats the steam-cycle condensate. Measurement errors stem from fuel property variation, occasional erratic instruments and changing ambient conditions, so readings are averaged over reasonable periods. Each HRSG has low and high pressure heat exchanger levels and a preheater: the LP level has a steam drum, evaporator and superheater, and the HP level a steam drum, economizer, evaporator and two superheaters. Because monitoring provides only inlet and outlet variables of the two pressure stages, not of each component, degradation is evaluated per pressure stage, as set out in the modeling section, without individual component degradation.

Degradation results come from actual data in the plant monitoring system, recorded hourly in two months (January and August) of the 2012–2013 period and then filtered using the proposed load determination criteria. The measured state variables used for modeling and degradation analysis, referenced to Fig. 1, are given in Table 1.

Seasonal ambient effects on HRSG performance are captured by collecting data in January and August, representing cold and hot ambient conditions. Setting a reference performance baseline is the first step of the degradation analysis and is essential to quantify component degradation.

Table 2 holds two groups: the actual test performance (ATP) recorded right after the plant was installed, and the modeling test performance (MTP), which is the model's reproduction of that test. In the ATP group, component performance comes from measurements at actual loads of 100%, 75% and 50%, and ATP is treated as the actual and most useful baseline over the plant's life. Since the plant does not measure inlet and outlet states of individual components within the HP and LP sections, degradation is applied to the complete low- and high-pressure stages as two units, together with the boiler feed pump.

The MTP group models the ATP data from the measured ATP variables plus assumptions from the literature. Because exhaust conditions leaving the HP-HRSG stage are not measured, they are set equal to those entering the LP-HRSG stage. As exhaust gas temperature changes little across the preheater and its inlet and outlet water enthalpies are similar, preheater degradation is not treated. Fig. 2 shows how HRSG efficiency varies with load, efficiency being heat output divided by heat input [19]. The exhaust gas and steam/water states of the ATP measurements serve as reference points for later data: when ATP state conditions are matched, the operating load is identified and degradation analysis follows, which keeps the degradation magnitude and trend free of fluctuation. Reference component performance is given in Table 3, and the 2012–2013 data are run through the model repeatedly to study component performance and degradation.

The exhaust specific heat is C_p,exh,(5,6) = C_p,a(5,6) + (f/(1 + f)) θ_exh,(5,6)   (2) (exhaust gas specific heat = air specific heat plus a fuel-air-ratio-weighted correction term θ).

C_p,a,(5,6), the air specific heat, is evaluated at the mean temperature of states 5 and 6: C_p,a,(5,6) = c_0 + c_1(T_(5,6)) + c_2(T_(5,6))^2 + c_3(T_(5,6))^3   (3) (air specific heat as a cubic polynomial in temperature), with T_(5,6) = (T_(5) + T_(6))/2 (mean of the two state temperatures), c_0 = 1.0189134 × 10^3, c_1 = −1.3783636 × 10^−1, c_2 = 1.9843397 × 10^−4 and c_3 = 4.2399242 × 10^−7.

The correction term is θ_exh,56 = CG_0 + CG_1(T_54) + CG_2(T_54)^2 + CG_3(T_54)^3 + CG_4(T_54)^4 + CG_5(T_54)^5   (4) (exhaust specific heat correction as a fifth-order polynomial in temperature), with CG_0 = 1.0887572 × 10^3, CG_1 = −1.4158834 × 10^−1, CG_2 = 1.9160159 × 10^−3, CG_3 = −1.2400934 × 10^−6, CG_4 = 3.0669459 × 10^−10 and CG_5 = −2.6117109 × 10^−14.

To get the fuel–air ratio f, the turbine polytropic efficiency is first expressed through the turbine pressure ratio: η_∞,t = (0.9 − (r_t − 1)/250) 100   (5) (polytropic efficiency in % falls linearly with pressure ratio). The turbine rotor inlet temperature then follows from T_(3) = T_(4) (r_t)^((n_g − 1)/n_g)   (6) (inlet temperature from outlet temperature and pressure ratio raised to the polytropic index), where the GT polytropic exponent n_g relates to the specific heat ratio γ_g via ((n − 1)/n)_g = η_∞,t ((γ − 1)/γ)_g   (7) (polytropic index relation for the gas), with γ_g taken as 1.33 [20].

The fuel–air ratio is f = (C_p,a,(1,2)(T_(2) − 298) − C_p,a,(1,3)(T_(3) − 298)) / (η_b (C_p,a,(1,3)(T_(3) − 298) + θ_exh,(1,3)(T_(3) − 298) − LHV))   (8) (combustor energy balance relative to 298 K solved for f), where LHV is the fuel lower heating value (kJ/kg), C_p,a(1,3) and θ_exh,(1,3) are taken at the mean temperature of states 1 and 3, and the burning efficiency η_b is assumed 0.98. Air and exhaust flows are then ṁ_a = (ṁ_f / f)   (9) (air flow = fuel flow divided by fuel–air ratio) and ṁ_exh = ṁ_a + ṁ_f   (10) (exhaust flow = air flow + fuel flow).

The low-pressure heat exchanger efficiency uses exhaust specific heats obtained in the same way: η_LP,HRSG = (ṁ_w,8 (h_s,7 − h_w,8) / (ṁ_exh C_p,exh78 (T_exh,7 − T_exh,8))) 100   (11) (LP stage efficiency in % = heat absorbed by LP water/steam over heat released by exhaust between states 7 and 8). Preheater: η_Preheater,HRSG = (ṁ_w,10 (h_w,9 − h_w,10) / (ṁ_exh C_p,exh910 (T_exh,9 − T_exh,10))) 100   (12) (preheater efficiency in % = water heat gain over exhaust heat loss between states 9 and 10).

Overall HRSG: η_HRSG = ((ṁ_s,HP (h_s,5 − h_w,6) + ṁ_w,8 (h_s,7 − h_w,8) + ṁ_w,10 (h_w,9 − h_w,10)) / (ṁ_exh C_p,exh(5,10) (T_exh,5 − T_exh,10))) 100 (equation number not printed; overall efficiency in % = sum of heat absorbed in HP, LP and preheater sections over exhaust heat released from state 5 to state 10).

paragraphs.section: HRSG performance modeling / Boiler feed pump (FWP)
paragraphs.text: Boiler feed pump (FWP): the actual hydraulic power consumed (the text refers to the CEP here) is Ẇ_BFP,ac = ṁ_m,9 v_9 (P_10 − P_6) / 100   (14) (pump power = mass flow × specific volume × pressure rise, divided by 100 for units). Degradation of each HRSG component is evaluated as HRSG degradation = ((η_HRSG(MTP) − η_HRSG(AP)) / η_HRSG(MTP)) 100   (15) (percentage degradation = drop of actual performance efficiency relative to the modeled baseline efficiency).

The modeling and degradation procedure was run on data from January and August over 2012–2013 for full and part loads, using the load determination criteria, and the main component results appear in Figs. 3 through 7. Each figure shows best fit lines versus time for the full and part load cases, and the R-squared value, a statistical measure of how well data follow the second-order fitted regression line, is boxed beside each line.

The boiler feed pump suffers fouling and problems such as impeller damage, bearing and seal wear, shaft misalignment and casing wear, which govern the rate and size of its performance loss. To limit stoppage and inspection difficulty, BFP degradation was assessed indirectly through its power consumption (Fig. 3). Consumption grew with operating time, by at most 1.34% at full load and 1.16% and 1.07% at 75% and 50% load. Degradation is clearly larger at full load and falls notably at 75%, while the 75%–50% gap is small compared with the 100%–75% gap; the rate starts fast and slows over time, and ambient conditions have no effect on BFP degradation. Fig. 3. BFP power degradation over two years at various loads.

HRSG back-pressure hinders exhaust flow through the unit and lowers output power by reducing exit steam enthalpy; it is lower in simple cycle mode and rises markedly in combined cycle mode. Fig. 4 shows back-pressure, measured as exhaust gas pressure at the HRSG inlet downstream of the expansion joint, across ambient conditions and loads. Due to HRSG degradation it rises with time by an amount depending on load, reaching 2.15% at 100%, 1.74% at 75% and 1.57% at 50% load, and its rate of increase slows over time. Fig. 4. HRSG back pressure degradation over two years at various loads.

Faults arise on the exhaust gas side (outer tube surface) and on the steam/water side (inner tube surface). Figs. 5–7 show HP and LP-HRSG efficiencies falling with time by load-dependent amounts, with no influence of ambient conditions on the trend. Outer-tube fouling, corrosion and fuel combustion deposits plugging the finned tubes, together with inner-tube scaling, corrosion from tube leakage and other problems, lower the efficiency of both pressure stages over time. The LP stage reduction peaks at −6.58% at the end of August-2013 at full load, against −5.13% and −4.35% at 75% and 50% load (Fig. 5).

Figs. 5 and 6 together show that HP-HRSG degradation also depends on load and that its rate declines with time. The HP trend follows the LP-HRSG trend, but LP degradation is larger since the low-pressure stage works with only a small temperature difference. HP stage degradation peaks at −5.6%, with −4.62% and −4.16% at 75% and 50% load. Fig. 5 and Fig. 6. Efficiency degradation of the low-pressure and high-pressure HRSG, respectively, over two years at various loads.

Fig. 7 gives the efficiency drop representing overall HRSG degradation over time, combining the effects of the LP and HP stages. Load again matters: the largest reduction is −6.02% at full load, against −4.42% at 75% and −3.9% at 50% load. As for the individual stages, the difference between full and 75% load is large relative to that between 75% and 50% over the same period, so degradation is highest at full load and the difference between loads diminishes as power decreases. Fig. 7. HRSG efficiency degradation over two years at various loads.

The study proposes full HRSG modeling and performance calculation, applied to HRSG measurements from 2012 to 2013, with degradation evaluated on January and August data to reveal the influence of operating and ambient conditions. HRSG faults were measured and computed, and the simulated degradation agrees with the open literature. Main findings: (1) BFP power needed for the required head and flow grew with time, most clearly at full load where the rise reached 1.34%, while the degradation rate fell with time. (2) Rising back-pressure reflects HRSG condition; it increased with time at full and part loads, most at full load with a maximum degradation of 2.18%, and less as load drops.

(3) Degradation of the two HRSG pressure levels, derived from their efficiencies using actual data, was greater for the LP-HRSG than for the HP-HRSG at every load, peaking at −6.78% for the LP stage and −5.61% for the HP stage at full load, and grew with time and load. (4) Considering the effect of component degradation on the overall HRSG criterion, both pressure stages behaved alike, degradation rising with time and load, with a maximum of −6.01% at full load and an amount governed by the operating load conditions.
